facts: The schwa is the most common vowel sound in English.

history: William Caxton set up England's first printing press in 1476. Printed books spread fixed spellings, even though the way people talked kept changing.
Between about 1400 and 1700, English long vowels slowly changed. Bite used to sound like "beet," and house sounded like "hoose." The sounds moved, but the spellings stayed put.
English borrows words from hundreds of languages and often keeps their spelling. That's why chef, choir, and yacht follow different rules.

ghoti.why: It doesn't really work. GH never says F at the start of a word, and TI only says SH before an ending like -tion. Still, it shows how strange English spelling can be.

iebefore.rule: I before E, except after C, or when sounded like A, as in neighbor and weigh.

list: If a word has one syllable, one vowel, and ends in one consonant, double the consonant before an ending that starts with a vowel.
X and W never double: fix → fixing, snow → snowing.
Drop a silent E before an ending that starts with a vowel. Keep it before an ending that starts with a consonant.
Noticeable and courageous keep the E so the C and G stay soft.
Change a Y after a consonant to I before most endings.
Keep the Y before -ing (cry → crying) and after a vowel (play → played).
Add -es instead of -s after s, x, z, ch, and sh, because you can hear an extra syllable.
English words almost never end in V, so a silent E comes along.
In English, Q is almost always followed by U.
Words borrowed from other languages can break it: Qatar, Iraq, qi.

farm.story: In 1066, French-speaking Normans conquered England. For hundreds of years, English farmers raised the animals while French-speaking nobles ate the meat. So we still have English names for the animals and French names for the food.
farm.caveat: That's the famous version. The novelist Walter Scott made it popular in 1819, and the real history is a bit messier, but the word pairs are real.
farm.tripNote: English often has three words for one idea: a plain one from Old English, a fancier one from French, and the fanciest from Latin.

cousins.fact: These words look alike because all of these languages grew from one ancient language, called Proto-Indo-European, spoken more than 5,000 years ago. Linguists rebuilt it by comparing its descendants, the way a detective rebuilds what happened from clues.
